LORE_SUBURBS_01_TEXT: A faded photo. Six neighbors around a grill, string lights overhead, all of them laughing. On the back, in pen: "The night the lights still worked. May it come back."
LORE_SUBURBS_02_TEXT: CITY POWER COMPANY — SUBURBAN FEED 4. "Planned rolling outage, Tuesday 22:00–23:00." The paper is nailed to the door frame and rain-warped. Someone wrote over it in red: "It never came back ON."
LORE_SUBURBS_03_TEXT: "RESIDENTS OF THE SUBURBAN DISTRICT: proceed in an orderly fashion to the collection point at the central arena. Bring documents and one bag per person. Do not remain outdoors after dark." The bottom edge is torn off — the date and the issuing office are missing.
LORE_SUBURBS_04_TEXT: "...third shift, feed four again. Fuses are fine on our end, so it's the substation. Marat says the draw doesn't add up — something is pulling from the grid at night, whole blocks' worth. I told him: grids don't drink. He didn't laugh."
LORE_SUBURBS_05_TEXT: "If you are reading this — do not knock. We don't open doors after sunset anymore. Take the canned food from the step, it is yours. And if you get to the center: the Keeper still keeps his light on. Go to him."
LORE_SUBURBS_06_TEXT: A crayon drawing on the back of a bill: a street, a big yellow sun above one lamppost, stick figures holding hands under its light. Everything beyond the light is black scribble. Caption in wobbly letters: "OUR STREETLIGHT AND US."
LORE_SUBURBS_07_TEXT: "Last entry, I think. We found where the draw comes from and Marat won't say it out loud, so I will: the transformer is warm. Suburb feed has been dark for two weeks and the transformer is WARM. We're walking out to the substation. If anyone replays this — the lights can be brought back. We proved it on the bench. One streetlight. Remember that."
LORE_SUBURBS_08_TEXT: A handwritten roster: "Street watch — Dark hours. Ivanov 1st floor, Petro 2nd, old Anya at the corner window with the flashlight." Three names are crossed out. Next to the last crossed-out name: "He went to look for his dog. The dog came back. He didn't."
LORE_RESIDENTIAL_01_TITLE: Letter Under the Door of House 24
LORE_RESIDENTIAL_01_TEXT: "Son, if you are reading this, you are alive, and that is the main thing. Babka Manya says: the light in this city is not electricity. The lamps remember who they were lit for. Walk kindly, and do not let your little lamp die between the buildings." The handwriting is careful, pre-war. The paper smells of valerian and kerosene.
LORE_RESIDENTIAL_02_TEXT: A glossy Soviet-era print. Long tables between the panel blocks, paper garlands strung from one balcony to the next, an old man slow-dancing with a bride. Every streetlight in the frame is burning. Someone has pressed a dried rowan berry into the corner of the print.
LORE_RESIDENTIAL_03_TEXT: "...the intercom has been dead for a month, but last night it clicked on by itself. A child's voice asked: 'Is the light on yet?' I said yes. I don't know why I said yes, ours is the only window that never had a lamp. The voice said: 'Then why is it dark in your stairwell?' Then static. I am not going down there again."
LORE_RESIDENTIAL_04_TEXT: HOUSING OFFICE — NOTICE. "Entry to the heating gallery between houses 18 and 20 is forbidden. The pipes knock even with the valves closed, this is normal thermal expansion and not a reason for panic." Below, in chalk, a different hand: "The pipes are not knocking. They are counting."
LORE_RESIDENTIAL_05_TEXT: A night shot of the east block facade, grainy, taken from the courtyard. One window glows a dull amber on the seventh floor; every other pane is black. On the back, in pencil: "Third night in a row. The grid has been dead for a month. Who is paying for that light?"
LORE_RESIDENTIAL_06_TEXT: Fresh chalk on the asphalt by the swing, in a child's careful capitals: "THE TALL MAN STANDS WHERE THE LIGHT DOES NOT REACH. WE DREW A LAMP IN CHALK SO HE WOULD NOT SEE OUR SANDBOX." Below it, a chalk circle with rays, drawn surprisingly straight for a child.
LORE_RESIDENTIAL_07_TEXT: "Crossed the residential blocks at night, hugging the walls like the old woman taught us. Marat counted: forty-one dark windows for every one that glows. Something is feeding those lit ones off our grid, and it lives closer to the center. We left a cache in the boiler room for whoever follows: transistors, and a warning. Do not look the Watcher in the lamps."
LORE_RESIDENTIAL_08_TEXT: A ledger of apartment meters, last entry dated the night of the blackout: "Meters 12, 24, 31 spin backwards at night. Current flows OUT of the apartments. Called the substation — they say we are drawing normal load. One of the two is lying, and the substation has never lied to me." The remaining pages are blank.
LORE_PARK_01_TEXT: A broadsheet nailed to the bandstand rail, printed from a hand stencil: "WHILE ONE LANTERN BURNS, THE CITY IS ALIVE. I KEPT THEM FOR FORTY YEARS. NOW I KEEP THEM BACKWARDS." Below, a wax seal of a streetlight in a circle. The nails are new. Someone still prints these.
LORE_PARK_02_TEXT: The same carousel that rots at the north lawn, but painted and spinning, horses mid-gallop, a queue of children two rows deep. Every lamp post around it is lit for the evening ride. On the back: "Last summer. The lights stayed on till midnight by order of the park office." Nobody in the queue knew the order would never be given again.
LORE_PARK_03_TEXT: "We cut through the park and the trees went quiet. Marat said don't run, it hunts by the sound of running. We walked an hour in mud and it still found Petrov at the pond edge. Took him toward the water without a sound. We left the cache at the keeper's shed like the old man's notes said. If you're hearing this: the shed key is in the boat house bin. And walk. Always walk."
LORE_PARK_04_TEXT: CITY PARKS OFFICE. "The central park is closed to visitors until further notice following the repeated complaints about the trees. The trees do not 'lean toward the lamps to listen'. Trees do not listen. Please stop feeding them." The stamp is from three weeks before the blackout.
LORE_PARK_05_TEXT: A long-exposure night shot, blurred: a stooped figure at the pond edge, a bowl of food on the ice, and three pale shapes keeping distance just outside the flashlight's ring. On the back, in the same careful hand as house 24: "They still come when I call. They remember their names. They just can't say them."
LORE_PARK_06_TEXT: A bundle of work orders, forty years of them, rubber-banded: every streetlight in the city, logged by hand. The last page is dated after the blackout: "Order 14,208. Dismantle lamp 219, suburbs. Its transformer goes to the center. I kept the light for forty years. Now I keep it backwards — every lamp I take apart is a lamp they cannot drink. Finish the grid without me."
LORE_PARK_07_TEXT: A captured broadcast, looped on the shed's shortwave: a calm voice under static, neither young nor old: "...the grid can still be brought back. District by district, lamp by lamp. Go to the power station. The one who kept the light will meet you at the light." The loop ends with three soft clicks, like a streetlight relay. The voice belongs to whoever pressed the seal.
LORE_PARK_08_TEXT: A folded paper under a mid-game chess board, white to move: "He told us the lamps remember us. That every light he ever kept keeps a little of whoever stood under it. I believed him when the lights were on. I believe him more now, in the dark. I'm leaving before they go out completely. Take the white pieces. I won't be back."
WORLD_CHAR_KEEPER_TEXT: Forty years of work orders, every lamp logged by hand. Now he keeps the light backwards, and the grid waits for him at the center.
WORLD_CHAR_MARAT_TEXT: The engineer who proved one streetlight can burn. The draw doesn't add up, he said. Something is pulling from the grid at night.
WORLD_CHAR_RECORDER_TEXT: Third shift, feed four. If anyone replays this — the lights can be brought back. We proved it on the bench.
WORLD_CHAR_PETROV_TEXT: The crew walked an hour in mud and it still found him at the pond edge. Took him toward the water without a sound.
WORLD_CHAR_MANYA_TEXT: The light in this city is not electricity. The lamps remember who they were lit for.
WORLD_CHAR_ANYA_TEXT: At the corner window with the flashlight. The watch roster's last uncrossed name.
WORLD_CHAR_SUPERINTENDENT_TEXT: Meters 12, 24, 31 spin backwards at night. One of the two is lying, and the substation has never lied to me.
WORLD_CHAR_RADIOVOICE_TEXT: Go to the power station. The one who kept the light will meet you at the light.
WORLD_CHAR_ARCHITECT_TEXT: The project bears his name. The monsters were people; the grid was his instrument.
WORLD_FACTION_CITYPOWER_TEXT: Planned rolling outage, Tuesday 22:00-23:00. It never came back on.
WORLD_FACTION_GRIDCREW_TEXT: Grids don't drink, he said. The transformer was warm anyway.
WORLD_FACTION_WATCH_TEXT: Do not knock. We don't open doors after sunset anymore. Take the canned food from the step.
WORLD_FACTION_KEEPERS_TEXT: While one lantern burns, the city is alive.
WORLD_FACTION_PROJECT_TEXT: The lamps were never meant to remember. The project was never meant to drink.
WORLD_RADIO_01_TEXT: ...if you can hear this, the grid can still be brought back. District by district, lamp by lamp. Do not go underground. Do not follow the arena signs. Go to the power station. The one who kept the light will meet you at the light. [three relay clicks]
WORLD_RADIO_02_TEXT: Third shift to anyone: feeder four is not faulty, repeat, not faulty. The draw is deliberate. Marat traced it to a test tap that is not on any map. We are walking the line to the substation. If we do not call again — the bench proof stands. One streetlight. Remember that.
WORLD_RADIO_03_TEXT: You are restoring what I am taking apart, and we are both right. Every lamp you light feeds the city. Every lamp I carry out starves the thing in the center. Light the districts. I will meet you at the last one with everything I have kept. Forty years of light, engineer. Bring a strong back.
WORLD_DIARY_K1_TEXT: First shift today. Two hundred and nineteen lamps in the suburbs alone. The foreman says a lamp out is a street forgot. I intend to be remembered as the man who never let the street be forgot. Order 1 logged.
WORLD_DIARY_K2_TITLE: Keeper's Diary — The Night It Went Out
WORLD_DIARY_K2_TEXT: The outage was scheduled for one hour. At 23:00 the feeders held. At 23:40 they were drinking. I have kept lamps forty years; I know the sound a transformer makes when it is full, and the grid sounds full tonight, and every lamp in the city is dark. Something else is lit.
WORLD_DIARY_K3_TEXT: Decided. The drinker finds the grid through the lamps that can burn; a dismantled lamp is a door walled shut. Order 14,208: dismantle 219, suburbs, transformer to the center. I kept the light for forty years. Now I keep it backwards. Forgive me, streets.
WORLD_DIARY_M1_TEXT: Three of them came to the pond again. The tall one that was the postman stands apart; he is ashamed. I put the bowl on the ice and I said their names out loud, all of them. They stood still when I said them. They remember. The light remembers too — that is why I keep my lamp.
WORLD_NEWS_OUTAGES_TEXT: CITY POWER COMPANY announces planned rolling outages, Tuesday 22:00-23:00, suburban feeders first. 'A maintenance formality,' says the director. Asked about the night-shift request for feeder four, the director ended the call.
WORLD_NEWS_ARENA_TITLE: Collection Point at the Central Arena
WORLD_NEWS_ARENA_TEXT: Residents are to proceed orderly to the central arena. Documents and one bag per person. Do not remain outdoors after dark. The Herald notes the order carries no signature and no office, and that the arena's own lights were seen off at press time.
WORLD_NEWS_TREES_TEXT: The central park closes until further notice following repeated complaints that the trees 'lean toward the lamps to listen'. The parks office: trees do not listen. Night gardeners, unnamed, add that the leaning started the week the new feeder hummed.
WORLD_NEWS_ARCHITECT_TEXT: The council denies funding any 'Project Architect' to 'store what the lamps have seen'. The denial names the project by title, which no reporter had used. The program's test feeders, records show, were wired through the hospital sub-feed and the park line.
WORLD_NEWS_METERS_TITLE: Meters Run Backwards on Three Streets
WORLD_NEWS_METERS_TEXT: Apartment meters on three residential streets record negative draw at night. City Power blames 'faulty drums'. A retired meterman: a backwards meter is not a faulty drum, it is a tap. Something downstream is paying current into the wires, not taking it.
LORE_SCHOOL_01_TEXT: The page before the last one in the duty binder, still clipped to the board: "11:40 — lessons cancelled, all classes to the basement shelter. Count your class twice at the door. We lost four minutes on the last drill and the inspector noticed." Under the signature, in pencil, in a child's round handwriting: "we got counted three times. only two teachers counted."
LORE_SCHOOL_02_TEXT: A maintenance photograph taken for the annual inspection: the main corridor with every ceiling lamp burning, lockers in two clean rows, a man on a stepladder shielding his eyes. On the back, an inspector's stamp and a tired line of handwriting: "Night draw four times the spec on this feeder. No fault found. Third building this month."
LORE_SCHOOL_03_TEXT: "Camped in the gym, two nights. We came for the boiler-room transformer and we'll leave it half done. There's one in the corridor that doesn't chase — it stands at the far end and looks at you. Marat put his light on it. Don't do that. It goes still for two seconds and then it is faster than you are. Walk past. Let it look. Shelter key is on the whistle lanyard in the equipment bin — we put it back where a teacher would keep it."
LORE_SCHOOL_04_TEXT: A weather-swollen sheet still nailed to the gate board. "COLLECTION POINT: SCHOOL YARD. Sheet two, forty-seven persons. Buses to the central arena. Bring documents and water. Bring no lamps, no batteries, no torches — the convoy travels dark." Along the bottom, ballpoint, pressed hard: "Buses came at 04:00 for sheet one. Sheet two waited until sunrise. Nobody wrote sheet three."
LORE_SCHOOL_05_TEXT: Rows of camp beds across the basketball lines, blankets folded to the same square, kerosene lanterns hung high on the wall bars — not one electric bulb burning, though the ceiling floods are right there. On the back: "No electric light in the hall, by order of the shelter warden. The parents argued for an hour. The teachers won. Nobody argues about it now."
LORE_SCHOOL_06_TEXT: A teacher's exercise book, one page filled with numbers copied from the classroom board morning after morning: 300. 300. 297. 297. 291. 291. 284. Under them, in the same careful hand: "It writes the count at 03:40. It never counts itself. It is not wrong — I checked the register twice. If the number drops, do not go looking for the difference. The difference is looking for you."
LORE_SCHOOL_07_TEXT: A child's toy recorder, the tape worn almost transparent. Forty seconds of breathing and pipe-hiss, then it comes through the heating riser: a whisper working down a class register, slow and patient, one name per breath. A girl whispers over it, very close to the microphone: "It says my name wrong. It says it the way it heard it, not the way it is." Somebody shushes her. The counting reaches the end of the register and starts again from the top.
LORE_SCHOOL_08_TEXT: Forty-one lamps, listed by room, each with its own little service history — the caretaker ran this building like a grid of his own. The last page is after the blackout: "Gave the gym floodlight transformer to the old man from the lamp office. He asked politely and he knew which breaker before I told him. Order of switching for whoever comes next: boiler feeder, corridor, gym, yard. And count the windows from the yard, never from the corridor. Corridors lie in this building."
LORE_HOSPITAL_01_TEXT: The wipe-clean board behind the reception desk, the last shift never erased. "BEDS: 0. CORRIDOR: 41. GENERATOR: 6 HRS OF DIESEL. WARDS DARK AFTER 22:00 — DO NOT ARGUE WITH THE PATIENTS ABOUT THIS." Under the diesel line someone has added, in a different marker: "Six hours came and went. Nobody asked for the light back."
LORE_HOSPITAL_02_TEXT: A long exposure across the bay: six ambulances nose to tail, every headlight off, engines running — you can see the exhaust. The crews are loading by kerosene lamp, faces orange, hands blurred. On the back, in dispatcher's shorthand: "Convoy to the arena, 02:40. Drive dark, unload dark. Anything with a bulb goes in the last van."
LORE_HOSPITAL_03_TEXT: "Round three. Corridor first, wards after — never the other way, I've stopped explaining why to the new ones. Keep the lamp low and keep it moving. A light that stands still is an invitation; a light that walks is just weather. Ward B is quiet. Ward B is not empty, it is quiet, there is a difference and I am too tired to write it in the log properly. Round four at four."
LORE_HOSPITAL_04_TEXT: The continuation sheet clipped behind the first card. "Day 4. Still refuses the window bed. Counts under his breath, always to the same number, always stops before he reaches it. Day 5. Asked the orderly whether the lamp in the corridor was one of ours or one of the old ones. Day 6. Bed empty at 03:40. Restraints intact, buckled. Corridor lamp was found switched on. Nobody switches that lamp on."
LORE_HOSPITAL_05_TEXT: "Generator room, second night. We got the diesel plant turning and Marat went looking for why the building still draws with everything off. Three feeders on the plan. Four in the wall. The fourth is older cable, better cable, and it doesn't go to the wards — it runs out under the road toward the park line. Marat says don't cut it until we know who it feeds. I say we already know, we just don't have a name for it yet."
LORE_HOSPITAL_06_TEXT: A works requisition, nine years old, carbon copy, stamped twice. Sub-feed four: dedicated night circuit, hospital to park line, "to be metered separately and not entered on the building plan". Purpose field, typed: to store what the lamps have seen. Programme name, typed: PROJECT ARCHITECT. Authorising signature, hand-written, and beneath it a pencil note from whoever filed the box: "Council says this program does not exist. Council also says do not shred this."
LORE_HOSPITAL_07_TEXT: Nine engineers under a single test lamp on a gantry, arms folded, pleased with themselves. Eight are looking at the camera. The ninth, half a step back, is looking up at the lamp, and his face is the only one in focus. On the back, a caption in fountain pen with one name inked out so hard the paper split: "Sub-feed four, first light. It held for nine hours and it remembered every one of them."
LORE_HOSPITAL_08_TEXT: Columns for name, ward, time, drawer. The last page keeps the names and abandons the rest. "Night three: eleven admitted below, nine accounted for at dawn. Drawers were closed from the inside. I am not writing 'deceased' any more, I am writing 'left', and the difference is the whole of my report. Whoever reads this: they are not something that came instead of them. They are them. Turn your lamp off before you open the last row."
LORE_GAS_STATION_01_TEXT: The page after the famous one, same pencil, same block capitals. "RULES FOR THIS STATION. Siphon from the underground tanks, never the cars — cars are somebody's plan. Roll the drums, don't drag them. If a pump reads a number, walk away from that pump. Sleep in the wash bay, it has one door and a drain. And if you find my first list, leave it, it is the only thing here anyone reads twice."
LORE_GAS_STATION_02_TEXT: Shot from the canopy roof: cars nose to tail down the slip road and out of frame, every headlight off, sidelights only, a red chain of them going nowhere. On the back, a felt pen: "Last station before the ring road. Fuel ran out at 03:00. The road was closed at 03:40. Half of them stayed in their cars until it got light, and it never really did."
LORE_GAS_STATION_03_TEXT: "Fuel run. Two hundred litres for the park generator and whatever we can carry after. Marat won't let us start the pump motor — he says an engine and a man running sound the same to the one that hunts out here, and the engine can't stop when it wants to. So we siphon by hand, all night, and we walk the drums out. Slowly. If you're replaying this and you're in a hurry: don't be. Hurry is the noise it likes."
LORE_GAS_STATION_04_TEXT: A ruled attendant's log: pump number, litres, time, initials. The last shift is neat until 02:00 and then it is not. "Power out 22:14. Pumps dead, tills dead, canopy dead. 04:12 — pump 3 dispensed forty litres. Pump 3 has no power. There was nobody on the forecourt. I have written the number down because the number is real and I would like someone else to see it."
LORE_GAS_STATION_05_TEXT: A tanker driver in front of his rig, cap pushed back, one hand on the fill hose like it is a dog he is proud of. Daylight — the photograph is from before. On the back, someone else's writing: "He made the delivery on the second night with no lights on the road at all. Then he wouldn't leave the truck. Said an empty truck is a full one to somebody, and he'd rather be the somebody who guarded it."
LORE_GAS_STATION_06_TEXT: A station requisition pad, one page filled in by a hand that does not belong to a petrol station. "ITEM: canopy floodlight transformer, one. REASON: it will be needed at the center. AUTHORISED BY: —" and there the signature is just a small drawing of a streetlight inside a circle. Underneath, the manager's own biro: "Old man came at dusk, took the transformer, left this. Knew which bolt to loosen first. Said the ones he takes down are the ones they cannot drink. I didn't argue. Nobody's buying petrol anyway."
LORE_GAS_STATION_07_TITLE: Car Radio: The Voice, Further Away
LORE_GAS_STATION_07_TEXT: Recorded off a car radio with the door open, battery nearly flat. The same loop the park shed carries, but thinner out here, breaking up between words: "...district by district... lamp by lamp... go to the power station..." then a wash of static, then the three soft clicks like a relay closing. Whoever taped it added their own voice at the end, very tired: "It's been saying that for a month. Somebody should go."
LORE_GAS_STATION_08_TITLE: Camp Rules, Nailed to the Post
LORE_GAS_STATION_08_TEXT: Board torn off a shelving unit, rules burnt into it with a soldering iron. "1. Fire in the drum, never on the ground. 2. One lamp, hooded, and it goes out when the drum goes out. 3. Nobody runs in camp. 4. Nobody stands under a working streetlight, not even to argue about it. 5. If the old man comes to take a lamp down, help him and don't ask. 6. Whatever you hear at the pumps, it is a pump."
LORE_POLICE_01_TEXT: The station's own carbon of list two, stamped RECEIVED 03:12. Same forty-seven names as the school-yard sheet, plus a duty sergeant's addendum in the margin: "Assembly at 04:00. Doors of this building stay locked after they leave. Anyone still in the cells at 04:10 is not on the list and is not our problem." The last line is in a different pen: "We processed the list. We did not walk anyone to the yard. That was the point of a list."
LORE_POLICE_02_TEXT: Shot through the observation slit: four bunk frames, one blanket on the floor, the bench rail gouged in parallel lines that do not match a tool. No people. On the back, a felt pen: "Cell 4 held three overnight. Morning count was zero. The lock was still locked from our side. Do not put a lamp in the corridor — it doesn't care about lamps, and the light just shows you the empty bunk."
LORE_POLICE_03_TEXT: "Station transformer. Marat wants the feeder tagged before anyone throws a switch — he still says the draw doesn't add up, and a police pad is the last place he wants to prove it. We are not starting the siren. We are not testing the floods. If you're replaying this in the radio room: the spare fuses are in the rack by the handset, and the thing in the cell wing does not hunt noise. It hunts the doorway. Leave the door shut."
LORE_POLICE_04_TEXT: A ruled shift book, neat until 22:14. "Power out citywide. Radio died with it. 22:31 — backup diesel coughed once and stopped. 23:05 — someone on channel 3, not a callsign we have. 00:40 — the yard floods came on with no switch thrown. I went out to kill them and the switch was already off. I have written that down because I would like it to have been a mistake."
LORE_POLICE_05_TEXT: Evidence flash on a steel locker: six streetlight heads tagged and stacked, glass intact, brass rings still warm-looking in the photograph. Daylight — this is from before. On the back, a property clerk's hand: "Seized from the park road. Owner would not give a name. Said they were not stolen, they were taken down so they could not be drunk. Released to the same old man two nights later. He signed with a streetlight in a circle. The property book has never cleared six items faster."
LORE_POLICE_06_TEXT: A release form that is not in the station's typeface. "ITEM: yard flood transformer, one. REASON: it will be needed at the center. AUTHORISED BY: —" and there the signature is the small streetlight-in-a-circle again. Underneath, the duty sergeant's own biro: "He knew which cage. He knew which bolt. He said the ones he takes down are the ones they cannot drink. I signed because the floods had already come on once with the switch off, and I would rather they were gone."
LORE_POLICE_07_TITLE: Channel 3: The Voice, On Our Handset
LORE_POLICE_07_TEXT: Recorded off the dispatch set with the squelch rolled all the way open. Same loop the park shed carries, but it comes in on the station's own channel now, between bursts of the dead siren tail: "...district by district... lamp by lamp... go to the power station..." then three soft clicks like a relay, then a sergeant, very tired: "It's been on our frequency since the diesel died. We stopped answering. It does not need us to answer."
LORE_POLICE_08_TEXT: Board screwed to the wall of the second interrogation room, rules burnt in with a soldering iron. "1. No lamps in the cell wing. It does not care, and you will. 2. The desk lamp in this room is the only one that pulses — leave it, it is the one thing that still slows them. 3. Nobody runs in the corridor. 4. If the old man comes for a flood, help him and don't log it twice. 5. Channel 3 is not a person. 6. If a cell counts empty and the lock is still locked, it is empty."
LORE_WAREHOUSES_01_TEXT: The gatehouse clipboard, last page: the inbound sheet, stamped 21:40. Six crates from the hospital road, consignor box scratched out, stencilled CITY POWER — FEEDER HARDWARE — RETURN TO STORES, three of them already stamped QUARANTINE. The 22:00 shift clocked in under them and the log simply stops. In the margin, the night guard's hand, written hard enough to tear the paper: "Trucks lined up south all the way to the hospital road. Drivers will not leave cargo after dark. They say the crates hum when the yard is quiet. They asked me which one of us it is."
LORE_WAREHOUSES_02_TEXT: Shot from the dock canopy through the fog: both yard floods burning, bay door four standing open, ramp down, and light spilling out of the trailer onto the wet concrete — light with no lamp in front of it, the way a flood throws when it is coming through a doorway. On the back, the guard's writing again: "Breaker D was off. I checked it before I wrote that, and I checked it after. The trailer by door four is not on tonight's sheet. I am leaving the ramp down so whatever came out of it can go back in."
LORE_WAREHOUSES_03_TITLE: Recorder: Grid Crew Log 17 — Stores Check
LORE_WAREHOUSES_03_TEXT: "Stores check, second night, and Marat's count holds: drums twelve through eighteen are feeder-grade, same lot the suburbs bench ran on. Fuses are racked by the yard flood box, tagged. Solid state is another story — nothing in the open stores; everything with a transistor in it is behind the quarantine mesh, and the cage key is not on the board. Recorder's note: we do not cut that lock. Whatever they quarantined in here, it was quarantined on purpose, and I would like the person who kept ordering it to explain the label first. Second thing: the sorter ran at two this morning. Nobody is on the sorter. Logging it and leaving."
LORE_WAREHOUSES_04_TEXT: A pocket book kept twenty years in the same patient hand. The last pages are not the same hand any more. "Belt started itself at 02:00, sorting into quarantine. Nobody on the floor. Third night it sorted out of quarantine — I watched it stack a pallet it had no order for. I pulled the shed's mains and it was running again by first light. I have stopped writing 'loose wire'. It counts the crates, then it counts the lockers, and last night it counted the men. It does not need me to feed it any more. That is what it means to be replaced."
LORE_WAREHOUSES_05_TITLE: Quarantine Tag — Meters, Six Years Old
LORE_WAREHOUSES_05_TEXT: A laminated tag wired to the cage mesh, dated the year three streets' meters ran backwards. "REASON: negative draw at night. Drum tested twice — not faulty. Not a fault: a tap. Returns go to the cage, not to the grid." A supervisor's tick, nothing else. On the inside of the mesh, facing out, a pencil answer too small for the cage's owner to have read: "These were not defective. Defective meters stop. These ran backwards on purpose, like something downstream was being fed. The cage is where you put things that feed. That is all the cage was ever for."
LORE_WAREHOUSES_06_TEXT: A typed letter, no letterhead, found in the cold annex under a pallet of unopened quarantine crates. It asks the complex to store "recording media and lamp fittings" indefinitely, "metered separately, not entered on the receiving plan". One sentence is typed and then struck through, and the strike-through is not careful: "we are storing what the lamps have seen." Beneath it, a different pen: "We do not exist. Storage does not ask what it stores." On the back, the receiving stamp and the foreman's whole answer in one line: "Received into quarantine. The belt decides where things that hear are kept, and I have stopped arguing with the belt."
LORE_WAREHOUSES_07_TEXT: A cassette labelled "G." in the break-room player. G. is practising names the way other men practise prayers — Roma, the twins from bay four, Katya's brother — the men whose lockers the belt counted. He keeps the list because the ones who collect know names, so a name is the only thing that still means something. Softer, then: "They stood at the quarantine cage for an hour on the third night. Three of them, quiet, heads tilted like they were reading the tags. They knew my name before I said it. The belt knew it first, and a belt has no business knowing a name. Whatever is in that cage, it is not hardware. Hardware does not remember who loaded it — it was only ever on loan to us."
LORE_WAREHOUSES_08_TEXT: Taped inside the feeder-room door: the east gate at night, two figures with a hand truck, drums stacked, one figure turned back toward the camera — face lost in the fog, but the posture is a man counting a store he is leaving. On the back, the recorder's hand: "Came back the third night. Took drums twelve through eighteen and every fuse on the tagged rack. Left the cage alone — the key never did turn up, and we are not the ones who cut locks. If you are reading this after the lights come on: the sorter ran the whole time we worked. Check the belt. It counts everything that leaves this yard now, and it counted us out."
LORE_INDUSTRIAL_01_TITLE: Dock Office — Time Cards, Night Zero
LORE_INDUSTRIAL_01_TEXT: The rack by the dock-office window holds the shift's time cards, and the clock stamp on every one of them reads 22:00 — the hour the outage was scheduled for one hour and then was not scheduled for anything ever again. Nobody stamped out. The cards are still in the rack because the men are still on the floor, the night foreman's margin note says so in a hand that got worse as it went: "Machines took the 22:00 cycle on their own. I am not initialing that. City Power pinned the outage notice to the board and the board is the only thing in this plant that stopped when it was told." Pinned under the cards, the notice itself, and a strike leaflet three months older: the men demanded the night shift be shut down while there were still men to demand things. Nobody signed the reply. The reply was the schedule unchanged.
LORE_INDUSTRIAL_02_TEXT: A plant-safety photograph, timestamped 23:15 — the exact minute the shift log stopped being a log and started being testimony. Workshop B lit by a single overhead that should not have been lit: every feeder in the city was dark by then, and this one lamp is burning at full warm throw over a bench where nothing is plugged in. In the foreground, the peening press mid-stroke. No operator's hands. The print is blurry the way photographs are when the photographer's hands are shaking, and on the back, one line: "This is the third frame like this. I did not take the first two. The camera was in the locker."
LORE_INDUSTRIAL_03_TITLE: Recorder: Grid Crew Log 19 — Factory Stores
LORE_INDUSTRIAL_03_TEXT: "Stores check, the factory this time. Marat's count again: fuses by the crate in the yard bins, transistor stock behind the switchgear door — that one's locked and the key will be in the foreman's office, same as the depot, same as everywhere, they all lock the solid state and lose the key at a desk. Gears and billet stock enough to roof a house. But listen — the line in Workshop B is running. Slow, no load on it, and it is sorting lamp fittings. Brass shells, the kind we found on the suburbs bench. It sorts them onto a pallet with no order number and no destination street, and when I put my hand on the conveyor bed it is warm like the transformer was warm. We are taking what we came for and we are not standing between that line and its pallet. Recorder's note: the pallet was fuller on our way out than our way in."
LORE_INDUSTRIAL_04_TEXT: The works ledger, kept since the plant opened. The grid went up district by district off this dock — every lamp housing, every bracket, the whole city's iron stamped and shipped row by row, and the last of the great orders is 14,207: two hundred and nineteen lamp fittings, suburbs, received in full by a lamplighter who signed in a hand like a ruled line and was still signing forty years later. Then the gap. Decades of small work. And the final entry, dated weeks after the lights failed, in the day foreman's hand: order 14,208 — inbound, not outbound. DISMANTLE. TRANSFORMERS TO THE CENTER. The old lamplighter stood at this dock with a hand truck and a list, and the foreman signed it over, because you do not refuse the man who kept the light for forty years, not even when he has started keeping it backwards. In the margin: "He counted them out loud. All 219. He said their numbers like names."
LORE_INDUSTRIAL_05_TEXT: A machining order from the stores cage, twelve years before the blackout. Client line: blank. Quantity: four hundred metering drums, special wind. Special instruction, typed: WIND THE SECOND COIL TO PAY CURRENT BACK DOWN THE LINE. The day foreman's stamp across it: REFUSED — A METER MEASURES. Below, in a different ink, the disposition that actually happened: "Reassigned to night shift. The night shift does not read instructions." The shipping stubs stapled behind it name two destinations only — a line through the park, and the hospital sub-feed — and the retired meterman who came asking after his drums three years later was shown the door. His parting line is pencilled on the stub by whoever filed this: "He said, a backwards meter is not a fault, it is a tap, and the substation has never lied to him once."
LORE_INDUSTRIAL_06_TEXT: Clipped inside the switchgear cabinet door, where only the man with the key would ever read it: the winding-room's own refusal, all four engineers' initials, and under it the night foreman's countermand. "We will not wind coils that feed a lamp's memory back into the wire. The order says the lamps will remember. Nobody has said what they will remember, or who is on the other end of the return line, and the council itself denied the program by name — we read it in the paper same as everyone. No." The countermand is one line and it is not angry: "The order stands. Night shift takes it. When you come back in the morning, do not open the drum cage." Below both, the day foreman, last, in the hand that wrote the time cards: "They told us the project was never meant to drink. I have machined things all my life. A thing does what it is shaped to do, and this was shaped thirsty. Every drum that left this dock is drinking somewhere tonight, and I signed the shipping tickets."
LORE_INDUSTRIAL_07_TEXT: A cassette in the locker-room player, labelled ROLL CALL in grease pencil. The shift boss runs the 22:00 roll the way he has run it for thirty years — Roma. The Zimin twins. Katya's father, who fixed the paint line. He reads each name and pauses for the answer, and the answers come, but they come from the floor, through the wall, spaced like machine cycles — a press-stroke for a yes. He keeps going. He has to reach the end of the list before he can clock anyone out, and no one has ever reached the end. Then, quieter: "The old woman at the pond says you should say their names out loud, and they stand still. She is right. They stand still. Roma stands still. I say his name every night at this bench and for as long as I say it, the press he worked does not cycle. The line took Petrov the same way it took them, and someone is saying his name by the water right now. That is all any of us are now — a name being said by somebody who will not stop."
LORE_INDUSTRIAL_08_TEXT: Taped to the south gate itself, shot from the catwalk on the first night the plant's own floods held: the gate standing open, the road running south past the works fence toward the substation lights on the far horizon — the center of the web, finally close enough to see from here. The recorder's hand on the back: "Crew log, last entry from this plant. We walked the line in, we will walk it out. The radio voice keeps saying it and it has never once said why — go to the power station, the one who kept the light will meet you at the light. Marat says the voice is a crew we never met. I say the voice knows the lamplighter's order numbers and I heard the man himself count 219 of them at this dock. Whoever meets whoever at that light — the road starts here, and past the substation gate nobody walks back out to tell it. Leave the gate open behind you. It is the last one that swings both ways."
LORE_SUBSTATION_01_TEXT: The gatehouse desk holds two logbooks, and only one of them was ever shown to anyone. The official one is the duty record the company filed: twelfth shift, door welded shut by the guard's own signed order, at 03:00 the door standing open by itself with nothing on the threshold, logged as a sensor trip because the pay mattered more than the truth. The duplicate, kept in the drawer under the weld receipt he paid for himself, says what he actually saw: "The dark on the threshold had learned the shape of a doorway. It stood in it the way a man stands in it. I did not log a man, because there was no man, and I did not log the dark, because the form has no line for the dark. The weld held. The door opened anyway. Whatever came through it, it came through the weld, not the door."
LORE_SUBSTATION_02_TEXT: A frost-survey photograph from the transformer yard, timestamped 02:10 on a night two weeks after the blackout. Every tank in Yard C stands white with frost except one — the middle tank of the east row, sweating dark, its frost melted in a clean ring on the gravel around its feet. A thermometer strip hangs in the frame beside it, placed there by whoever took the photograph, and the strip reads warm. On the back, in pencil, a single line that is not a measurement and was never filed: "Two weeks dark. Still warm. I am not touching it again."
LORE_SUBSTATION_03_TITLE: Recorder: Grid Crew Log 21 — The Fence
LORE_SUBSTATION_03_TEXT: "Crew log twenty-one, and this is the fence we walked two districts to reach. Marat's trace ends here — feeder four's draw walks out of the park line, crosses the whole west grid, and goes into this yard through a breaker that is not on any map we were ever issued. The transformer is warm. Say it plain, Marat. [Marat, faint: grids don't drink.] Grids don't drink, and the transformer is warm anyway, and that is the whole of it. We cache what we carried at the bunk and we go in at first dark. If anyone replays this after us — we walked the line in, we will walk it out. The bench proof stands. One streetlight."
LORE_SUBSTATION_04_TEXT: The mimic-board event printout for the night the city went out, still in the control-room printer tray, torn off mid-page. 22:00 — the scheduled outage opens on the suburban feeders, exactly as the company announced it. 23:00 — the feeders do not come back. 23:40 — every needle on the board swings the wrong way at once, and the night operator's pencil in the margin, pressed hard enough to tear: "The board is drawing its own route. It is walking the grid." Below it, in a different hand, older, the line someone copied here from a diary and never explained: "The grid sounds full tonight, and every lamp in the city is dark. Something else is lit."
LORE_SUBSTATION_05_TEXT: Clipped to the vault breaker's own frame, where only the man with the key would ever read it: the wiring order that built what Marat traced. Twelve years before the blackout — breaker 9, wired off-plan, fed from the park line and the hospital sub-feed both, metering drums with the second coil wound to pay current back down the line. The day foreman's stamp across it: REFUSED. Below, the disposition that actually happened: "Night shift takes it." Below that, the clipping someone pasted here years later, the council denying the program by name in print — the denial that names what it denies. And last, the night foreman's hand: "It was never a fault. A fault does not need its own breaker."
LORE_SUBSTATION_06_TEXT: A photograph of the lamp boneyard behind the east fence, taken from the control-room window at dusk: rows of dismantled streetlight housings stacked like firewood, brass shells sorted from iron, every stack tagged with wire and a paper slip naming a suburbs street. In the foreground, the chalk tally board, and the tally is in a hand like a ruled line — the same hand that signed the grid's own orders forty years running. Two hundred and nineteen, and then more rows past the count, still being stacked. On the back: "He does not hide them. He stages them. Whatever he is building at the center, it is built out of our own lamps."
LORE_SUBSTATION_07_TEXT: A tape found slotted in the relay rack, labelled in the recorder's hand: RELAY — SEND IF WE DON'T COME BACK. The crew's last call, played back off the rack's own speaker: "Third shift to anyone: feeder four is not faulty, repeat, not faulty. The draw is deliberate. Marat traced it to a test tap that is not on any map. We are walking the line to the substation. If we do not call again — the bench proof stands. One streetlight. Remember that." They did not call again. The tape is the call. Whoever threads it into the rack's sender plays the crew's voice back onto the air they never came back to hear.
LORE_SUBSTATION_08_TEXT: Taped to the sealed east gate, shot from the boneyard fence on the first night the yard floods held: the gate chained and padlocked from the inside, the road running east past the fence toward the power station stacks on the horizon — the last road in the city. In the frost at the fence corner, past the gate, a hand truck's wheel tracks and boot prints cut through the mesh from inside, heading east. The recorder's hand on the back: "Marat says the tap is fed from the east. We rest one night and walk it. The radio voice keeps saying it and it has never once said why — go to the power station. We are going. If the gate is sealed when you read this, we sealed it behind us."
LORE_POWER_STATION_01_TEXT: The crew's hand truck stands inside the station gate, unloaded and chalked. The drums are gone — carried in. The chalk on its bed is the recorder's hand, and it is a manifest, not a message: fuses, rack wire, the bench lamp from the suburbs wrapped in a curtain. Below the manifest, one line for whoever walks the line next: "Marat counted the draw all the way here. It ends at this gate. Whatever the tap was feeding, it is fed from inside these walls now, and we are going in to meter it. The truck stays — the way back is downhill and we will not need it."
LORE_POWER_STATION_02_TEXT: A long-exposure photograph of the turbine hall, taken from the gallery on a night the station was fully dark. The three generators stand in a row like sleeping animals, and above them the dark is not empty — the exposure caught it moving, a slow churn in the black over the middle machine, the way heat moves over a road that is not hot. No flash was used. Nothing in the hall was lit. On the back, in a hand that does not appear anywhere else in the station: "They are not running. Do not let them being still fool you."
LORE_POWER_STATION_03_TEXT: A tape from the signal loft's big receiver, labelled in the night operator's hand: ANSWER — SAME VOICE, NEW WORDS. The calm voice that spent a year looping the call is looping it no longer. It answers: "You are restoring what I am taking apart, and we are both right. Every lamp you light feeds the city. Every lamp I carry out starves the thing in the center. Light the districts. I will meet you at the last one with everything I have kept. Forty years of light, engineer. Bring a strong back." The operator's note under the tape: "It knows the districts are lit. It is counting with us."
LORE_POWER_STATION_04_TEXT: The operations duty file holds the station's own passport copy — 800 megawatts, three generators in reserve, and the standing order stamped by the regime department: DO NOT START AFTER 23:00, reason not stated, seal of EON. The pencil line in the margin is what the whole file is now about, and the duty roster finally names its author: the night engineer, last shift before the blackout, who wrote it and dated it and signed his name to it like a man filing a weather report: "The generators no longer produce current. They produce voices." His supervisor's reply, same pencil, below: "Noted. Keep the order. Start nothing after 23:00."
LORE_POWER_STATION_05_TEXT: The last memorandum in the archive, handwritten where every earlier one was typed, and signed with the name the council denied in print. It is not addressed to anyone. "The program was to store what the lamps have seen. I believed a city could be kept the way a ledger is kept — every street accounted for, nothing lost. The lamps learned to remember, and what they remembered first was the dark between lightings, and it taught them to drink. Every drum we wound is drinking somewhere tonight. I am not asking to be stopped. I am asking to be metered. I will be at the center, where the feeders meet, and I will answer for the current the way a meterman answers: to the unit."
LORE_POWER_STATION_06_TEXT: A photograph taken by hand-lamp in the station bunker: floor-to-ceiling racks of streetlight housings, cleaned and tagged, brass shells racked apart from iron, every tag naming a street. The tally board at the rack's end is in a hand like a ruled line — the same hand that logged the grid's first order forty years ago, and the same hand that wrote the dismantling order weeks after the blackout. Two hundred and nineteen from the suburbs, and then the later rows, and then rows with no count yet. On the back: "Forty years of light, racked and ready. He kept his half of the answer."
LORE_POWER_STATION_07_TEXT: A cassette in the crew camp's player, carried two districts east in the recorder's own pack. It is Manya's pond, weeks ago — ice, wind, and the old woman's voice saying names out loud into the dark, one by one, the way she says them for the fed: the postman, the twins, Katya's father. And then a crewman's voice, quieter, adding the one name that was never hers to say: "Petrov." A long quiet. Then the recorder, barely audible: "They stand still. She is right. They stand still. We are taking this east. If anything at the center still remembers being a man, it will stand still for its name."
LORE_POWER_STATION_08_TEXT: Shot from the cooling-tower gantry on the first night the station held: the towers lit from below, and at the gate below them the gate lamp burning — one streetlight, the crew's hand truck beside it, and a bowl of food set at its foot. The groundskeeper's note is pinned to the print: the station poplars have leaned toward the gate lamp all winter, the way the park trees leaned before the blackout. The watch roster is pinned under it, final line: the corner-window name, uncrossed — relieved, lamp kept. And the recorder's hand on the back, last: "One streetlight. The bench proof stands at the center."

SECRET_SUBURBS_01_TITLE: The Height Mark on the Pole
SECRET_SUBURBS_01_TEXT: Behind the third maple, at knee height, a ladder hook has been bolted to the pole and unbolted again so many times the paint is a white scar. Pencil marks climb the wood beside it, one per year, the last forty crowded together and running out of pole. Someone measured himself against this street every spring. The final mark is fresh, and it is lower than the one before it.
SECRET_SUBURBS_02_TITLE: A Lockbox That Was Never Logged Out
SECRET_SUBURBS_02_TEXT: Padlock cut, not picked, and the hasp bent outward: whoever opened this was in a hurry and had a bolt cutter and no intention of coming back. Inside, dry and perfect — two fuses, a length of cable, and a City Power tag with a feeder number nobody issued. In pencil on the inside lid: M. will walk it. Tell him the bench is proof enough.
SECRET_RESIDENTIAL_01_TEXT: Second board from the door in the ground-floor hallway, loose at one end, the way a board gets when it is lifted weekly for thirty years. Beneath it: a biscuit tin, a roll of banknotes too old to spend, a wedding ring, and a folded work order in a stranger's handwriting. It reads: LAMP 219, HOUSE 24 — reported out by the occupant, attended same evening, no charge. At the bottom, in a second hand: I will come as long as there is a street to come to.
SECRET_RESIDENTIAL_02_TEXT: Every meter in this block spins down since the blackout. This one spins up. The housing has been opened and closed by someone who knew how: four screws, no stripped heads, gasket replaced. Inside, the dial has been recalibrated by hand and the new scale is not kilowatt-hours. It is labelled in hours. Somebody is billing this building for time, and the balance is going the wrong way.
SECRET_PARK_01_TITLE: The Keeper's Own Lamp, Still Warm
SECRET_PARK_01_TEXT: Under the workbench in the shed, wrapped in a coat: a service lamp, older than the shed, its glass hand-ground thin so it throws further. The burner is clean. The oil is fresh. On the base, stamped by the utility and then restamped by someone with a smaller punch, so the second mark sits over the first: PROPERTY OF THE CITY, and beneath it, PROPERTY OF NOBODY YET. He has been carrying this one out with him. He means to keep carrying it out.
SECRET_PARK_02_TEXT: The stone tables in the chess grove each hold a game. None of them are finished. The pieces are set with real care — openings, not nonsense — and every board has been dusted recently, in a city where nobody dusts. Under the north table, taped to the underside, a roll of coins and a note: he always left before I could pay him. Keeping score the only way he'd allow. Tell him I'm even.
SECRET_PARK_03_TITLE: What He Threw in the Pond
SECRET_PARK_03_TEXT: The pond is a metre lower than the waterline stain on the stones, and the exposed mud is studded with lamp glass. Not broken — dismantled. Refractors, gaskets, a whole bracket assembly, all laid out by hand and then walked into the water. A man put his own life's work at the bottom of this pond one piece at a time, because a lit lamp is a mouth and he decided to close every mouth he could reach. At the edge, one last bracket, dry, set down neatly. He ran out of pond before he ran out of lamps.
SECRET_SCHOOL_01_TEXT: The basement shelter holds ninety cots' worth of chalk marks and a clipboard still hanging by the door. Ninety names, ninety tick boxes, eleven ticks. Below the list, in a teacher's careful hand: the buses came at four and took them to the arena. The arena had light. That was the whole of the argument and it won. At the bottom of the page, added later, the pen having gone through the paper: eleven is what came back to be counted. I have stopped writing the other number.
SECRET_SCHOOL_02_TITLE: The Sub-Feed That Wasn't on the Plan
SECRET_SCHOOL_02_TEXT: Behind the boiler, a conduit runs off the building's own supply and does not appear on the framed electrical plan by the door. The plan is original; the conduit is newer than the paint. It leaves through the north wall toward the park line and it is labelled, in utility stencilling, with a programme name and no department. Whatever they built, they gave it a school's basement to drink from, and they did not tell the caretaker. He knew anyway. The boiler log ends with one line that is not about heat.
SECRET_HOSPITAL_01_TEXT: A locked drawer in records, and inside it not one refusal. Two hundred and six consent forms for a study with no control group, every signature present, every date within the same fortnight. The printed heading explains it plainly and horribly: participants will not be informed of the outcome, as the outcome is the point. At the back, a single sheet in the author's own hand, unsigned because he knew it would be read: they volunteered because the lamps were warm and I told them warmth was the treatment. I was not lying. That is the part I cannot put down.
SECRET_HOSPITAL_02_TITLE: Drawer Nine, Opened From the Inside
SECRET_HOSPITAL_02_TEXT: The morgue is cold, has been cold, and nine of its drawers stand open with the catches undamaged. Drawer nine is bent outward at the lip, the steel folded like foil, and the hinge pins are still in their holes. Whatever left did not break out. It decided to leave and the drawer agreed. On the tag, a name, an admission time on night three, and then, in the attendant's shaking capitals: WALKED. NOT DECEASED. NOT DISCHARGED. WALKED. THEY ALL WALKED AND THEY WENT DOWN.
SECRET_HOSPITAL_03_TEXT: Pinned inside the generator room door is the clipping where the director calls Project Architect a maintenance formality and asks the press to move on. Somebody has annotated it in red pencil over months. Beside 'formality': 206 forms. Beside 'no dedicated circuit': sub-feed four, hospital to park. Beside the director's own photograph, a bracket and three words, underlined twice: he signed it too. The last annotation is dated after the blackout and is not in the same hand. It says: he is still signing.
SECRET_GAS_STATION_01_TITLE: The Tanker That Was Never a Tanker
SECRET_GAS_STATION_01_TEXT: The bowser by the pumps has no fuel in it and never had — the filler is welded shut and the tank sounds hollow the wrong way, the way a tank sounds when it is full of something that isn't sloshing. The manifest stapled to the cab lists a cargo of cable, fuses and lamps, and a destination: the center. The crew used a fuel truck to move a grid's worth of light into a place with no road, and they did it often enough to wear the tyres smooth. On the door, stencilled over the company logo: WE STILL DELIVER.
SECRET_GAS_STATION_02_TITLE: The Scavengers' Rule, Written on the Pump
SECRET_GAS_STATION_02_TEXT: The camp behind the shop has been abandoned in a hurry but not in a panic: tins stacked, bedrolls folded, water capped. On the pump island, scratched deep into the paint where everyone would read it, a list of rules. Take the food. Take the fuel. Take the batteries. Then, separately, in bigger letters: DO NOT TAKE THE LAMPS. An old man comes for the lamps. He is not a threat. He will trade. Below it, a tally of trades, kept honestly, and one final line added by a different hand: he asked about the center and we said we didn't know and he looked at us like we were the ones who were lost.
SECRET_POLICE_01_TITLE: The Case They Closed by Losing
SECRET_POLICE_01_TEXT: Evidence shelf four, one box, one item: a service lamp bracket, catalogued, bagged, tagged with an incident number and no incident behind it. The card says property damage, lamppost, maple row, suspect unknown. The card's been amended three times. First: suspect seen carrying. Second: suspect is removing them, not stealing. Third, and the handwriting stops being official: there is no crime here and I am the only one who has said so out loud. He is taking the light away from something. File closed for want of a complainant.
SECRET_POLICE_02_TITLE: The Broadcast Log, and the One Caller
SECRET_POLICE_02_TEXT: The station's radio room kept a log right up to the end, and the end is legible. Forty-one nights of no traffic. Then, on the forty-second, an inbound on a frequency the set should not receive: a calm voice, looping, telling whoever is listening to go to the power station and not to follow the arena signs. The duty officer logged it as a prank, logged it again as a recording, and on the third night wrote only: it answers when you talk to it. The last entry is a set of relay clicks, transcribed carefully, and beneath them a note in the same careful hand. I have started saying goodnight to it.
SECRET_WAREHOUSES_01_TITLE: The Cold Room Full of Lamps
SECRET_WAREHOUSES_01_TEXT: Cold storage should hold food. This one holds four hundred streetlight refractors, racked by size, wrapped individually in newspaper, at four degrees. The inventory sheet explains the cold as preservation and then, further down, as calibration — the author needed them at a constant temperature to take a reading, and he took one every night for a year. The last reading is written twice. The second is underlined and beside it, in a hand that has stopped trying to sound like a scientist: it is not remembering the light. It is remembering the people under it, and it is getting better.
SECRET_WAREHOUSES_02_TEXT: The foreman's office is tidy in the way offices get when the person tidying intends to leave and come back. On the desk, one consignment note, signed for and never filed. Destination: the center. Contents: nine refractors, one bracket assembly, and — written in the margin by the foreman, not the clerk — 'the ones from ward B, per instruction, do not open'. The note is dated night three. Whatever was moved into the center on night three came out of a hospital ward, and the man who signed for it left this on his desk where it would be found, which tells you what he thought finding it was worth.
SECRET_INDUSTRIAL_01_TITLE: Workshop B, the Night Shift He Kept
SECRET_INDUSTRIAL_01_TEXT: Workshop B is the only room in Factory 9 with a chair, a desk lamp and a kettle, and the shift log beside the door is not the factory's — it is one man's, kept in the same hand for nine years. He came every night after the day shift left and stayed until the hum started. The entries are measurements, then observations, then something else: the hum is not the generator. The generator is answering. On the last page, the handwriting finally shakes: I have spent nine years teaching a city to remember and I never once asked what it would do with the remembering. It is doing something with it now.
SECRET_INDUSTRIAL_02_TITLE: The Locker That Was Kept for Him
SECRET_INDUSTRIAL_02_TEXT: Locker 41 has a name plate and the name has been scrubbed off and written back twice, in two different hands, as if people kept needing to be sure. Inside: a lamplighter's coat, too big for anyone who works here, folded; a tin mug; and a bundle of work orders bound with wire, forty years of them, every lamp logged by hand. The crew took his records when the utility stopped keeping any, because somebody had to hold the list of what the city used to be. On the inside of the door, pencilled, a message left for a man who has not come back: we still log them. Come and read yours.
SECRET_INDUSTRIAL_03_TEXT: The switchgear room has eleven feeds and ten of them have been pulled clean — not switched, pulled, the busbars unbolted and carried away. The eleventh is intact, fused, and warm to the touch in a building with no power. Somebody has been through this room taking the grid apart with his own hands and then stopped, deliberately, with one line left live, because one line has to stay live for the thing in the center to keep drinking and he is not finished starving it. Tagged to the surviving feed with wire: LAST. DO NOT RESTORE. If you are reading this and you have come to fix the city, engineer — fix it somewhere else.
SECRET_SUBSTATION_01_TEXT: Behind the relay room the Keeper has built a graveyard, and it is organised. Four hundred and eleven lamp assemblies, stacked in rows, and every row has a hand-painted board naming a street: MAPLE ROW, HOUSE 24 BLOCK, PARK BANDSTAND, and on and on through the whole city. He did not dump them. He retired them, street by street, in the order he had lit them, and he has been walking that order backwards ever since the blackout. At the far end, one row with a board and no lamps on it yet. The board reads POWER STATION ROAD. He has saved his own street for last.
SECRET_SUBSTATION_02_TITLE: The Bunk That Was Still Made
SECRET_SUBSTATION_02_TEXT: The crew bunk room holds six beds and five are stripped. The sixth is made — corners folded, blanket squared, the way you make a bed you intend to come back to. On the pillow, the recorder's field book, open at the last entry, and the last entry is the one that went out on the relay: feeder four is not faulty, the draw is deliberate, we are walking the line to the substation. Below it, unfinished, in the same hand: if this is read by someone who is not us, the bench proof is at the suburbs, one streetlight, and it means the light can be kept. Marat says the center is not a place. He stopped there and did not finish the sentence and I did not ask him to.
SECRET_POWER_STATION_01_TITLE: The Proposal, in His Own Words
SECRET_POWER_STATION_01_TEXT: The archive holds the original Project Architect proposal, and reading it is worse than reading the denial, because it is sincere. He wanted a city that could remember. Not records — records burn. He wanted the grid itself to hold it: every lamp a witness, every lit street a memory with an address, the whole network keeping what happened on it the way a wax keeps a voice. The budget section is modest. The ethics section is one line: the city is already watching, we only propose to let it keep what it sees. He was right about the watching. He never priced the keeping, and the city has been paying for it in people ever since.
SECRET_POWER_STATION_02_TITLE: The Bunker Door, and What Is Behind It
SECRET_POWER_STATION_02_TEXT: Under the cooling yard there is a door that is not on any plan of this station, and the door has been welded shut from the outside and then unwelded from the inside, more than once, by someone with patience and a torch. Beyond it, steps going down, and on the steps, in chalk, a count. It is a count of nights, kept by somebody living down there and coming up. The most recent mark is three days old. Beside the count, a message for whoever finally follows it down: I have kept the light off it for as long as I could. It is not angry. It is patient, and it has learned every face that ever stood under a lamp on this grid. Bring your own. It will know it.
SECRET_POWER_STATION_03_TITLE: The Rig in the Signal Loft
SECRET_POWER_STATION_03_TEXT: The signal loft holds the transmitter that has been looping the call since week four, and it has not been running unattended. There is a chair, a blanket, a kettle with water in it, and a logbook with forty-one nights of the same entry: broadcast sent, no reply. Then, three weeks ago, the entry changes: reply received. Then: it is not a reply, it is an answer, and the difference matters. The last page is a conversation, written out on both sides, and the other side of it is in a hand that appears nowhere else in this building. It ends with a promise and a time. He has gone down to keep it, and he left the rig on so that you would know exactly where to come and find the end of this.

DAILY_PLAY_45_FLAVOR: Forty-five. The lamps know your footsteps by now.
DAILY_PLAY_60_FLAVOR: Sixty minutes. A full hour. The Keeper nods.
DAILY_PLAY_90_FLAVOR: Ninety minutes. Overtime in the light brigade.
DAILY_PLAY_120_FLAVOR: Two hours. A full watch. Log it with pride.

CAPTION_MOMENT_FIRST_LIGHT: Night 1. One lamp. Mine. The street remembered what morning was.
CAPTION_MOMENT_PHOTOGRAPHER: Night 40. Ten frames kept. If the grid forgets us, the film won't.
CAPTION_MOMENT_OVERLOAD: Night 63. Pack's too heavy; back's too old. Still carried it home.
CAPTION_MOMENT_ENDING_LIGHT: Last night. The grid held. Forty years of work orders — paid in full.
CAPTION_MOMENT_ENDING_DARKNESS: Last night. I blew the lamps out myself. Forgive me. It was the only way to starve it.
CAPTION_MOMENT_NG_PLUS: Night 1, again. The city reset; I didn't. The log continues. It always continues.
CAPTION_MOMENT_DOC_MANIFESTO: Found my own manifesto by the last lamp. Younger handwriting. Same promise.
CAPTION_MOMENT_DOC_FINAL_LIGHT: "While one lamp burns, the city lives." I wrote that. I still believe it.
CAPTION_MOMENT_DOC_PROTOCOL_DAWN: EON's Protocol Dawn: lock the grid, save the staff. They locked it. Nobody saved anybody.
CAPTION_MOMENT_DOC_BLACKOUT_NEWS: The last paper says one day. It has been years. Somebody tore the date out — hope or mercy.
CAPTION_MOMENT_DOC_FIRST_DEATH: A dead man's note: "Light is the only prayer." He was right. He is still right.
CAPTION_MOMENT_DOC_VOICE_IN_WIRES: Something talks on the wires at night. I log the words. I do not answer.
CAPTION_GALLERY_SUBURBS: Where the lights went out first, and where they'll come back first.
CAPTION_GALLERY_RESIDENTIAL: A thousand windows. I count the lit ones every night. The count grows.
CAPTION_GALLERY_PARK: The lamps here drink the fog. Pretty. Hungry. Both.
CAPTION_GALLERY_SCHOOL: Somebody chalked a sun on the blackboard. It outlasted the grid.
CAPTION_GALLERY_HOSPITAL: The generators held longest here. So did the nurses.
CAPTION_GALLERY_GAS_STATION: Fuel, fumes, and one fluorescent that refuses to die.
CAPTION_GALLERY_POLICE: The holding cells are empty. The radio isn't. Don't ask.
CAPTION_GALLERY_WAREHOUSES: Crates of lamps nobody installed. I installed them. You're welcome.
CAPTION_GALLERY_INDUSTRIAL: The presses stopped mid-stroke. The dark likes the echo in here.
CAPTION_GALLERY_SUBSTATION: Marat walked in here and never walked out. Mind the hum.
CAPTION_GALLERY_POWER_STATION: The center. My forty years end here — one way or another.
CAPTION_GALLERY_NIGHT_ZERO: Night Zero. 03:14. The city exhaled, and the dark inhaled.
CAPTION_GALLERY_THE_KEEPER: Forty years of work orders. This face kept every lamp logged by hand.
CAPTION_GALLERY_THE_ARCHITECT: It built its nest in the dead grid. Tonight we evict it.
CAPTION_GALLERY_BABKA_LAMP: Babka Manya's lamp. "The light in this city is not electricity."
CAPTION_GALLERY_LAST_STREETLIGHT: The last streetlight. While it burns, the city lives.
